EssayOct 21, 2026

Elizabeth Holmes

An uncomfortable mirror

I watched the Elizabeth Holmes documentary yesterday, You can see everything, by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. I watched it at the theater, meaning I drove into town specifically to watch it. I had to know... what kind of documentary film has spoilers? Spoilers you have to conscientiously avoid online? I found my seat in the second to last row and was held there, riveted for over three hours without a bathroom break. Damn, now I get it. But that's not exactly what inspired me to write this morning. It's more that, even before watching the documentary, I know what Elizabeth Holmes' story means to me. I know what it reflects in my understanding of the world and - to be real - in myself. And watching the documentary exposed even more of that reflection. I'm sure we will all see different things when we watch the movie, like watching through slightly different mirrors, blurred and distorted by our own experiences. I want to describe my imperfect view, because there's something there that I suspect is universal.

I have no idea where to start. Grad school? My first internship out of high school? That messed up Lasers in Surgery and Medicine conference in Florida? My first year at Apple? Fuck it, it doesn't matter. The point is we all learn somewhere along the way that we need to master the masquerade of egos, buzz words, and hype. Like that time I sought advice from these two older white guys at an Incubator in St. Louis, Missouri, and was told in barely coded language that I didn't have it. It had nothing to do with the idea I had spent years developing, prototyping, and studying. In keeping with the spirit of the documentary, I won't go into the actual idea. You can read about it here if you want.

By contrast, Elizabeth Holmes has it. And if I could speak directly to the start-up incubators and investors for a minute, Elizabeth Holmes is exactly the person you've been grooming. She mastered your masquerade - and possibly nothing else. What do you see when you look into the mirror of her ballistic success and downfall? Void of anything else, she reflects something very uncomfortable in us, without the alluring distortions needed to maintain our shared illusion. Surrendering to her narcissists - her Sunnys, her Billys, she exposes our patriarchal underbelly and finds a hollow refuge. Now she is doubling down on tech start-up culture, feeding its needs like another narcissistic lover, and we watch her in the documentary traumatize herself again and again. As Nathan Fielder intuits, she sticks David Blaine's ice pick into her hand over and over again, convincing us it's a magic trick when in fact it's all real.

So is Elizabeth Holmes my femme fatale? I'll pass, thanks. Whether playing victim or aggressor, she sustains the tempers of narcissism and patriarchy, exposing it to us and then charming us all into complicity. Which leads me to the next reflection I see in Elizabeth Holmes - my own. For all my inadequacies in the game, I still play. I traumatize myself over and over again, navigating the use of my emotions for my own gain, the use of my vulnerability to garner support. As an autistic person, the concept of "my own gain" may be different than most... I love being right, but I do not feel any victory in winning an argument when I'm wrong, and my standard for right and wrong can be brutal. All the same, I try and mimick to the best of my ability the tricks of the trade. After my first year at Apple, I dissociated from the effort. To this day, I can't remember who I was that year. Over the following years, I graciously discovered that I didn't have to play that game to be successful. I didn't have to agonize over losing an argument of words, a contest of egos. I didn't have to exert faux authority to be respected by my peers. I feel immense gratitude for the people who taught me this, just by embodying it themselves. What does that part of my story have to do with Elizabeth Holmes? Maybe nothing. But when I see how differently she purports herself now - post Theranos, post trial, post motherhood - I see the dissociation I experienced myself. I wonder if anyone on the outside would believe this version of me if they had met me before. What I project onto Elizabeth now is dissociation not only from the past version of herself but from the belief in her own autonomy.

Autonomy - such a tricky concept for those of us socialized as women. If you haven't experienced it, I can understand why you might not believe it. The collective gaslighting is beautifully alluring. When you asked to cut the grass when you were six, did your dad say no to protect you from cutting your toes off? Did he then encourage your brother to do it when he was five? Did he take your brothers out camping, teach them to tie knots, build a fire, set up a tent, catch fish, while asking you to stay home so your mom could watch Little Women with her daughter? When you entered engineering school with all-male peers, who had spent years fixing up engines with their dads, did you question if you were good enough? When did you start opting out or curling up in the comfort of being taken care of? And when did you learn that your looks and your body were the means to be safe in the world, like a token to trade in for being kept in a cocoon of dependence and blamelessness? When your dad told your fiancé sternly to take good care of you, did you feel the last of your sense of autonomy evaporate in a wave of warmth and love? If it were expected of you, would you accept the freedom to pursue your interests, at the cost of agency over your body and your life decisions? Respect and compassion to those of us who say no. It's not an easy road to retain your sense of self in the onslaught of a loving patriarchy. Reject the carrot and the stick falls on you like an anvil.

As I watch Elizabeth in her relationships, with her fiancé Billy and even with her interviewer Nathan, I see her pour herself into that patriarchal cocoon, with the trust and naïveté of someone who desperately seeks to free herself of the illusion of autonomy. Will we accept this version of her? If she lobotomizes self-empowerment and agency from her image, real or imagined, will we see her humanity? Watching this dollhouse mother, deferential in her support of the worst of our inclinations, I find I don't care if the act is real or performative. Because either way, she is showing us a very real manifestation of our subconscious beliefs and the unwritten rules of our culture.

I reflect a lot on my complicity. As we put Elizabeth Holmes in prison and tell ourselves that she is different than we are, do we allow ourselves to see it? Or do we excise not the worst of ourselves but the mirror that reflects it? When we 'can see everything', do we revel and gape, only to look away?

From a comfortable distance, only indirectly affected by her actions, I can allow her story to pull me into myself, and it exposes within me a deep emotional well, that ultimately has nothing to do with her and everything to do with the echoes in my own experience. Deliberate self-absorption may be the only way through.

Nathan concludes his documentary with footage of he and Elizabeth swimming in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego. They appear as lovers, playfully clinging to each other as the waves envelop them again and again. Eastern philosophy teaches that we are not our actions or our thoughts; rather, we are pure truth, consciousness, and bliss. It teaches that we find bliss equally in perfect ignorance as in perfect self-awareness. Seeing them in this way, I wonder whether we are watching the embrace of illusion or our true nature, whatever is left when the mirror evaporates.
